planting.note: Set container-grown offsets in spring into sharply drained, gritty or rocky soil in full sun; established plants shrug off brief freezes into the low 20s F once rooted.

directions: Hedgehog Agave forms a dense, symmetrical ball of slender, outward-curving leaves tipped in soft (non-rigid) spines, giving the whole rosette a bristly, sea-urchin look distinct from the broad-leaved agaves. It is one of the more compact species suited to small xeriscape beds or large containers, slowly clustering into a mounded colony of rosettes rather than staying solitary. Plant in lean, mineral soil with excellent drainage and keep irrigation minimal; wet winter soil is a far greater threat than Gulf Coast summer heat. Give it an open spot away from taller perennials so the rosette keeps its tight, rounded form.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant offset divisions in late spring once soil has warmed; protect from hard freezes below the mid-20s F for the first few winters.

directions: This variegated selection of the Oaxacan species Agave guiengola carries broad, glaucous blue-gray leaves edged in a wide cream-to-butter-yellow margin, making it one of the showier variegated agaves for a sunny bed or large pot. It offsets freely, and because many of the pups emerge variegated themselves, a single plant can be divided over the years to multiply the display. Grow it in fast-draining, lean soil and resist the urge to overwater or over-fertilize, which softens the leaves and dulls the coloring. Where winters dip below the mid-20s F, grow it in a container that can be moved under cover.

planting.note: Root individual pad cuttings in dry, gritty soil after the last frost; allow the cut edge to callus for a week before setting the pad in soil.

directions: Named for its unusually long, narrow, strap-shaped pads that curve and lengthen like a cow's tongue, this Texas native form of Engelmann's prickly pear grows into a sprawling, mounding thicket useful as an impenetrable barrier hedge in a sunny xeriscape bed. Bright yellow spring flowers are followed by purplish-red summer fruit that is edible once the glochids are removed. It tolerates Gulf Coast humidity and clay-alkaline soils far better than many Opuntia as long as drainage is adequate, and it recovers quickly from hard pruning if it outgrows its space. Give it room to spread, since old clumps can reach several feet across.

planting.note: Transplant into a raised, gritty bed or container in spring; keep dry through winter dormancy to avoid rot.

directions: Snowball Cactus earns its name from a dense covering of fine white radial spines that nearly obscure the globular stem, giving small clusters the look of a pile of snowballs even in the middle of a Gulf Coast summer. A ring of pale pink to white flowers appears near the crown in late spring, followed by small pink fruit. Because it is more cold-sensitive than many landscape cacti, grow it in a raised, fast-draining bed or a container that can be sheltered when a hard freeze threatens. Keep it bone dry over winter and resume light watering only after nighttime temperatures stay reliably above the mid-40s F.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root leaf or offset cuttings in dry, gritty mix in spring; wait until the cut callouses before placing on soil.

directions: A hybrid of Echeveria purpusorum and Echeveria derenbergii, this cultivar forms a tight, hen-and-chicks rosette of pale grey-green leaves that blush pink to coral at the tips and keel during cool weather. Clusters of small orange, bell-shaped flowers rise on short stalks in spring above the foliage. It is a good choice for a sunny succulent border edge or container grouping where its compact size and winter color can be appreciated up close. Keep soil on the dry side and provide bright, direct sun to prevent the rosette from stretching and losing its tight form.
sources: Illustrated Handbook of Succulent Plants: Crassulaceae
Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Transplant rooted offsets in spring into rocky, caliche-like soil; avoid any bed that holds moisture after rain.

directions: Native to the rocky limestone slopes of the Big Bend region, this clustering hedgehog cactus is covered in a dense, interlocking mass of tawny, rust-colored spines that give the whole stem a russet glow distinct from the straw or white spines of related species. Rust-red flowers with darker midribs open at the stem tips in mid-spring and last only a few days each. It needs a rockier, more mineral soil than typical garden beds provide, so a raised scree or gravel bed works far better than amended topsoil. Established clusters are tough and long-lived but slow growing, so start with the largest clump available for the best display.
